title: How Mail Order Marriages Work
summary: Josh and Chuck examine mail order marriages (international marriage brokerage): the murky mix of genuine love matches and exploitation. They cover the definition of the practice, its colonial American origins (government-encouraged brides for lonely settlers, tobacco wives in Virginia), the western frontier schemes (ASA Mercer's bride brokering, women's rights activism of Mercer girls), the rise of matrimonial personal ads in the nineteenth century, early twentieth-century anti-Asian immigration laws tied to picture-brides and the Gentleman's Agreement, the paper-catalog era and modern online agencies, the Immigration Marriage Fraud Amendment and conditional residency, the International Marriage Broker Regulation Act of 2005, statistics on immigrant abuse and murders of mail order brides, LGBTQ use of the practice, and male mail order husbands in Ireland. A listener email closes the show urging COVID vaccination.

segments.title: Opening and defining mail order marriages
segments.summary: The hosts frame the episode as murky, noting both genuine love matches and exploitative cases, and define mail order marriages as international marriage brokerage where spouses are often largely unknown to each other. They note the industry's size and that it is bigger in Taiwan and South Korea.

segments.title: Colonial American origins and Buying a Bride
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Marcia Zug's book Buying a Bride and early colonial shortages of women, including government encouragement of brides and inheritance-based incentives for widows, plus tobacco wives in Virginia who had to donate tobacco to the Virginia Company.

segments.title: Western frontier brides and ASA Mercer
segments.summary: As settlement moved west, rowdy male populations led to laws and schemes to attract women, especially in California and Washington Territory. ASA Mercer recruited women from back east, and some Mercer girls later became abolitionists and suffrage advocates, including Mehitable Haskell Elder, who organized a women's rights conference with Susan B. Anthony.

segments.title: Matrimonial ads and the marriage-for-love shift
segments.summary: Matrimonial advertisements in London and then America in the nineteenth century gave women some choice of suitors. Magazines dedicated to matrimonial ads appeared, but the practice was criticized and stories of swindled people were popular in newspapers.

segments.title: Early twentieth-century immigration laws and anti-Asian politics
segments.summary: Mail order marriages shifted to overseas brides in the twentieth century. Congress passed restrictive laws such as the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882; the 1907 Gentleman's Agreement allowed Japanese wives of men already in the US to immigrate, a loophole later closed in 1924. Critics accused brides of seeking green cards or being sex workers.

segments.title: Power imbalance, dependence and modern safeguards
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the power imbalance mail order brides face due to language, isolation, and financial dependence, and how this can resemble trafficking under broad definitions. They also note women's own agency in seeking better lives.

segments.title: Catalog era, online agencies, costs, and the 2005 regulation act
segments.summary: Describes the old catalog subscription model of the seventies and eighties and modern online agencies with fees and tours, including Vietnam's illegal but widespread industry. Internet tools now let women vet men, and the International Marriage Broker Regulation Act of 2005 required agencies to give background information after high-profile murders.

segments.title: Immigration fraud rules, data, and abuse statistics
segments.summary: Explains the Immigration Marriage Fraud Amendment of 1986 and the two-year conditional residency that leaves brides dependent. Cites estimates of immigrants via brokers and studies of spousal abuse, and discusses murder statistics of mail order brides versus general married women, arguing about moral panic.

segments.title: LGBTQ use and male mail order husbands
segments.summary: The practice was extended to same-sex couples after the Supreme Court struck down parts of DOMA, and some LGBTQ people from countries without rights use it to escape danger. The hosts mention male mail order husbands in Ireland.
